newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korean churches offer safe haven for activists.
newsitem.headline: South Korean churches offer safe haven for activists.

text.p: By offering sanctuary to strike leaders at Seoul's Myongdong Cathedral, the Roman Catholic church is upholding a long tradition in South Korea of providing succour to opponents of the government.
It has also dramatically displayed the influence of Christianity over politics in an Asian nation where more than a quarter of the population goes to church.
South Korea boasts the world's biggest Christian congregation at the Yoido Full Gospel Church where 500 pastors care for 700,000 faithful and direct 11 choirs.
It has more Roman Catholic saints than any non-European country and its leading politicians are devout church-goers, including President Kim Young-sam, a former Presbyterian deacon.
Kim's chief political opponent, Kim Dae-jung, is a Roman Catholic.
Myongdong Cathedral has emerged as the focus of anti-government protests linked to the passage of a new labour law that has sparked three weeks of strikes.

Beneath a statue of the Virgin Mary, seven leaders of the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions are camped out in a ramshackle tent, leading wildcat strikes with portable telephones and evading arrest.
Myongdong clergy leave little doubt where their sympathies lie in a stand-off over the labour law and another law boosting the power of a domestic security agency.

"Lord, you know better than anyone the suffering of the workers and pain of those unfairly persecuted under the security laws," intoned a white-haired priest reciting mass to a crowd outside the gothic church on Monday.
"Please give us strength to fight against injustice."
The first Catholic missionaries landed on the Korean peninsula in the 1780s.
"From the beginning of Catholic history here in Korea, the church reached out to farm workers, the slaves, the disposessed, to give them hope," said Sister Susana Youn.
"It was a forum for social justice at a time when there wasn't any recourse. People who became Catholics were often persecuted and sometimes martyred for their beliefs."
When Pope John Paul II visited in 1984 he elevated 103 martyrs to the sainthood.
Activists have often received shelter under the red-brick walls of Myongdong Cathedral, and the imposing structure in a commercial district has become a symbol of democratic struggle.
It has not always been able to guarantee safety. In 1995 riot police stormed the grounds, dragging away Korea Telecom union leaders protesting privatisation plans.
"The workers have no place to go. By being with them like this, we create a space for them, give them legitimacy," said Father Donal O'Keefe.
O'Keefe's organisation, the Catholic Priests for the Realisation of Justice, led Monday's mass on a stage draped with banners reading "We don't want a civilian dictatorship".
Father Moon Jung-hyun roused the crowd with roars of "Dissolve the New Korea Party!", referring to the ruling camp.
"In Korea the social status of priests is still very high," explained Youn. "So they can say things that others are thinking but cannot express."
Up to 14 million South Koreans profess to be Christians, almost outnumbering Buddhists. Churches are immensely wealthy and some control lucrative business empires.
The dramatic growth of Christianity has paralleled South Korea's economic takeoff since the 1950s.
